problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$
